Chapter 7: The Economics of Dispossession—Wealth, Poverty, and the Price of Progress.
Money. It’s often the quietest force in the story of Indigenous and settler relations. You don’t always see it, but it’s there—moving quietly behind the scenes, shaping decisions, justifying actions, and leaving its fingerprints on every community it touches.
When you look at the history of North America, it’s impossible to ignore how much of it is really a story about wealth—who had it, who lost it, and who was denied it.
Picture this: there’s a small town, bustling with life, built on land that once belonged to a nearby Indigenous community. The town seems to have it all—shops line the streets, roads are smooth, schools are full of resources. But just a few miles away, the original community is struggling. Their schools are underfunded, their infrastructure is falling apart, and opportunities feel out of reach.
The difference is clear if you stop to look. But most people? They just drive by, not thinking twice about why one place is thriving while the other is just fighting to get by.
The truth is, the wealth of entire nations was built on land and resources taken from Indigenous peoples. Gold, timber, oil, fish—all these riches were extracted, sold, and profited from. But fair compensation? That was rare. Treaties might've promised payments, but those payments were often tiny, delayed, or sometimes never made at all.
What’s left is a legacy of poverty—not by chance, but by design.
And for many families, the struggle isn’t just about money. It’s about dignity. Imagine a parent standing in line at a government office, filling out form after form for assistance. The questions feel invasive, the process is slow, and even when help finally comes, it’s never quite enough. You can’t help but wonder—why is their community always at the end of the line, always having to ask, always being told to be grateful for scraps?
But despite all that, there are powerful moments of resilience. You might see a group of young people starting a business, blending traditional knowledge with new ideas. Or an elder teaching others to harvest wild rice—turning an ancient skill into a new source of income. Communities look out for each other, share what little they have, and keep building for the future, even when the odds are stacked against them.
Here’s something to pay attention to: the outside world usually just sees poverty. They don’t ask about the reasons behind it. They might talk about “handouts” or “dependency,” blaming individuals instead of the systems that created these challenges in the first place. The real story is about wealth being taken, resources transferred, and opportunities shut off.
But there’s more to the story than just loss. New possibilities are starting to take shape. Some Indigenous communities are negotiating better deals when companies want to extract resources, insisting on a real share of the profits. Others are investing in education, language revitalization, or cultural tourism—reclaiming what was lost and building something new.
The path isn’t easy. There are a lot of obstacles. But the determination to create a better future? That’s strong, and it’s growing.
In the end, the economics of dispossession isn’t just about numbers on a page. It’s about something deeper—about who gets to dream, who gets to build, who truly gets to belong.
And while the price of progress has been painfully high, the story isn’t over yet. The future’s still unwritten.
